rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four real routes into coverage and knows exactly where each one lives: the regulatory split in "Whoop ships an FDA-cleared ECG and a blood-pressure feature that is deliberately not a medical device" is the cleanest story in either set. B is solid, but "Whoop ships FDA-cleared ECG — after the competition already did" invents named rivals and leans on unsupplied differentiators like "screenless band" and "subscription model" as if they were in the brief. A also does the adult thing: it names the holes without decorating them.
gaps_in_A: "a feature nobody has cleared" overreaches slightly; the update only says Whoop's blood-pressure feature is not diagnostic and competitors already ship cleared ECG, not that nobody has cleared any cuffless blood-pressure product.
"newsjack-detector" as the next step is a bit process-heavy for a launch-only update; useful if seeking external pegs, but a founder could also go straight to regulatory or accountability outreach.
The paywall angle asks "how many members sit on the top tier"; useful proof, but the update gives no membership base, so this may be hard to substantiate before the launch window closes.
gaps_in_B: "Apple Watch / Samsung / Fitbit feature race" names competitors the update did not name. The set later says named rivals are needed as proof, but the angle already smuggles them into the beat framing.
"screenless band" is not in the supplied update. It may be true of Whoop, but this exercise demanded grounding in the update, not brand memory.
"form factor" and "subscription model" are plausible differentiators, but not supplied facts; B uses them to rescue the late-entrant angle instead of treating them as open proof needs.

B skips the strongest angle A found: the single-launch regulatory split between FDA-cleared ECG and deliberately non-medical blood-pressure insights. That is sharper than another catch-up-in-wearables frame.
